body.text: In Brief:
• Trump's toughest move yet against the ICC could complicate Australia's position.
• Allies have condemned the sanctions, while Australia weighs its response.
The United States has sanctioned the International Criminal Court (ICC), just hours after a Nobel Peace Prize decision that appeared certain to anger US President Donald Trump.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the US would ban transactions with what he called a "rogue court", vowing to cut off its resources and cripple its ability to operate in an escalation of a long-running campaign against the Hague-based tribunal.
"Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC," Rubio said.
Trump later turned his anger on Norway, branding the Nobel committee's choice of South African jurist Navi Pillay a "disgraceful and embarrassing decision".
The move puts Australia, a US ally and founding supporter of the court, in a difficult diplomatic position as key allies split over how to respond.
What the sanctions do
The ICC tries individuals suspected of the world's most serious crimes, including war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide.
The Trump administration has already sanctioned 17 people linked to the court, including its prosecutor and several judges.
The latest step goes much further, potentially punishing companies that provide services to the institution itself.
Jared Mondschein, director of research at the United States Studies Centre, said the move represented a significant escalation.
"This is perhaps the most aggressive move yet," he told SBS News, noting that earlier measures targeted individuals rather than the court as a whole.

US sanctions typically bar US-based companies from conducting business with a sanctioned organisation, forcing banks to shut accounts, insurers to end coverage and software companies to halt cooperation.

Court officials have been preparing for months for the prospect of sanctions on the court itself, shifting office computers from Microsoft software to open-source alternatives and making new arrangements for banking and health insurance.

The latest measures include a six-month grace period and exemptions for telecommunications, software, pension payments and detainee-related transactions, something Mondschein described as a window for negotiation.
Why is Trump sanctioning the ICC?
US wariness of the court is not new and has historically crossed party lines, Mondschein says.

"Both Democratic and Republican presidents have been concerned about the ICC and its jurisdiction over US citizens," he said, noting the US signed the Rome Statute that established the court but never ratified it.
The US has also long opposed efforts by the court to investigate alleged crimes involving American personnel in Afghanistan.
The ICC has issued an arrest warrant for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu over alleged crimes in Gaza.
"I think more than anything else, the goal is for the ICC to stop trying to prosecute US citizens as well as allies of the United States, including the leadership of Israel," Mondschein said.
"The Trump administration has concerns about the political bias of the ICC and it being overzealous in its prosecution of targets that are more politically motivated than legally motivated."
The US also has a law dubbed the "Hague Invasion Act", allowing it to use "all means necessary and appropriate" to defend US personnel or allies detained by the ICC.
What's the Nobel Prize got to do with this?
The announcement came just hours after the Nobel Peace Prize was awarded to Navi Pillay, the South African jurist best known for her work in international human rights law.
Pillay, 85, spent much of her career defending anti-apartheid activists and last year, chaired a UN commission of inquiry that found genocide was occurring in Gaza.
Israel has rejected those findings.
Jorgen Watne Frydnes, chair of the Norwegian Nobel Committee, said Pillay had been "instrumental in ensuring that war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocide are prosecuted".
He said awarding the prize to Pillay was "a clear message to those who are putting pressure on these institutions, to those who are sanctioning the judges and are attacking the institutions".
Speaking after the award, Pillay said: "We are living through an era when international law and human rights are under significant political attack".
Israel condemned the award as the "grotesque weaponisation" of a prize to legitimise "anti-Israel hatred".
Pillay also appeared to acknowledge Trump's long-running interest in the Nobel Prize.
"If you clap a little bit more, I may share this prize with Trump," she joked during a standing ovation.
Trump responded by saying the Nobel Prize had been "forever discredited" and claiming he had "never heard" of Pillay.
"This is an indelible stain on the country of Norway and those people that made such a disgraceful and embarrassing decision," he said.
Mondschein said Pillay was a well-known critic of Israel, an issue that has long been a source of friction between the Trump administration and international legal institutions.
The award to Pillay was also a pointed snub to Trump, who had spent two years lobbying for the Nobel Prize.
'Tension' for Australia
The ICC has 125 member states, including Australia.
Canada, France, Germany, Japan and the United Kingdom said in a joint statement they "strongly disagree" with the sanctions.
The European Union said it was "ready to take any necessary measures" to ensure the court could continue operating.
Australia, a founding supporter of the ICC and a key US ally, now faces a diplomatic balancing act, Mondschein said.
"It's a tension for Australia. It's also a tension for Japan," he said, noting the ICC's current president is Japanese.
Australia has not yet publicly responded to the sanctions.
"I don't think Australia has been in favour of these actions by the Trump administration," Mondschein said.
"They have been critical of them, perhaps not as critical as other countries.
"But this is something I don't think Australia really wants to telegraph too early.
"If anything, they want to consider all their options moving ahead."
The ICC said its future "now rests also in the hands of the states that created it".
"History will judge this moment."
— With additional reporting by Agence France-Presse and Reuters
